+strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Isa.66.24	unquenched fire and dead rebels	Isaiah leaves the rebels as corpses while their worm does not die and their fire is not quenched; 87:13 makes the sufferer himself unable to die, so the bodily condition is the pointed difference within the shared enduring-fire scene.
+strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Targum Jonathan on Isaiah 66:24	Gehenna gloss, soul not dying, unquenched fire	Targum Jonathan's Gehenna paraphrase turns Isaiah's displayed corpses into sinners whose soul does not die while their fire is unquenched; that Jewish interpretation comes unusually close to the commentary's conscious, unending state in the fire.
+strong	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Babylonian Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 17a	Gehinnom consumed but certain sinners remain	In its reading of Isaiah 66:24, the Bavli says certain apostates descend to Gehinnom for generations and that Gehinnom is consumed while they are not; it explicitly develops the asymmetry of lasting punishment without the punished passing away.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.9.43	enter life or Gehenna's unquenchable fire	Jesus contrasts entering life with being cast into Gehenna's unquenchable fire; that direct life/fire antithesis sharpens the commentary's claim that the fire of 87:13 is a place where the condemned does not live.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.9.48	worm does not die, fire not quenched	Mark retains Isaiah's imperishable worm and unquenched fire; it is a close Christian formula for punishment that never runs down, alongside the commentary's renewed torment and never-arriving death.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Rev.9.6	people seek death but cannot find it	In an apocalyptic plague people long to die, but death flees them; this is a direct, though temporary, counterpart to the commentary's picture of agony in which death is wanted or approaches yet never arrives.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.14.11	fire, everlasting smoke, no rest day or night	The worshippers of the beast are tormented and have no rest day or night; its denial of repose closely meets the commentary's expansion of not dying into no easing, sleep, or stillness.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Luke.16.24	conscious anguish in flame	The rich man remains conscious and cries out that he is in anguish in flame; this supplies a narrated Christian analogue for the commentary's insistence that fire's occupant is not extinguished by suffering.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Luke.16.26	fixed chasm, no passage out	Abraham describes an impassable chasm that prevents passage from the place of torment; it specifically parallels the commentary's repeatedly frustrated desire to leave the fire.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.46	eternal punishment and eternal life	Matthew's final judgment places eternal punishment and eternal life in one antithetical sentence, a close frame for the commentary's contrast between enduring torment and the real, lasting life denied to it.
+strong	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Rev.20.14	lake of fire called the second death	Revelation names the lake of fire the second death, whereas 87:13 carefully says that its inhabitant does not die there; the contrast shows two different theological ways of naming fire's finality.
+strong	incil	yorum_gelenegi	Augustine, City of God 21.3	resurrection body enduring eternal fire	Augustine argues that the damned can suffer bodily fire without their bodies being destroyed; this patristic explanation directly addresses the commentary's problem of pain persisting while death never completes.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Job.3.21	longing for death that does not come	Job describes sufferers who dig for death but do not find it; although it is not a hell scene, the denied release provides a concrete analogue for the commentary's death withheld amid affliction.
+medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.11.11	death spoken of as sleep	Jesus calls Lazarus's death sleep before explaining that Lazarus has died; it closely supports the commentary's secondary sense of death as sleep and rest, which is unavailable in the fire.
+medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.14.13	the dead in the Lord rest from their labors	The blessed dead are said to rest from their labors, furnishing the positive counterpart to the commentary's claim that the one who cannot die in the fire is also denied rest.
+strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	WLC:Isa.26.14	dead do not live, shades do not rise	Isaiah says of hostile rulers that they are dead and will not live or rise; the negative Hebrew life verb closely matches the life/death language, but punishment here is exclusion from resurrection rather than 87:13's deathless suffering.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.26.19	your dead shall live and arise	Isaiah's answer to the preceding no-life statement is that God's dead will live and arise; it supplies the positive resurrection horizon against which the commentary distinguishes a fire that grants neither death nor life.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.12.2	awakening to everlasting life or contempt	Daniel's sleepers awake either to everlasting life or everlasting contempt; this gives a biblical two-outcome resurrection frame for the commentary's opposition between full afterlife and enduring punitive condition.
+strong	tevrat	karsi_anlati	2 Maccabees 7:14	martyr's resurrection to life and tyrant's exclusion	The martyred brother expects resurrection to life from God but tells the persecuting king that he has no resurrection to life; its death-to-life contrast illuminates the commentary's peaceful death-and-rising figures over against the doomed state.
+strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Rev.1.18	the living one became dead and lives forever	The risen Jesus names himself the living one who became dead and is alive forever; this compact death-life-resurrection sequence is the positive inverse of 87:13's suspended condition.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.6.9	raised Christ dies no more	Paul says that the risen Christ dies no more and death no longer rules him; it provides a Christian account of deathlessness joined to actual life, precisely the conjunction the commentary says hell lacks.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Cor.15.22	in Adam all die, in Christ all made alive	Paul binds Adam to universal death and Christ to being made alive; this directly meets the commentary's Adam-to-earth sequence of death and eventual resurrection, rather than an ultimate state without either.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rev.21.4	no more death in the renewed creation	In the new creation death, mourning, crying, and pain are removed together; it supplies the positive destination in which no death means healed life, contrasting with the fire's deathlessness without life.
+strong	tevrat	soydas	WLC:Deut.30.19	Arabic h-y-y and m-w-t, Hebrew hayyim and mavet	Moses sets life and death before Israel and commands them to choose life; the Hebrew life/death pair is cognate with the Arabic roots named in the commentary and makes ethical response determine which side is inhabited.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.33.11	turn from the wicked way and live	God calls the wicked to turn from their way and live; this closely parallels the commentary's moral reading in which turning from the reminder yields a final state without life.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.1.28	rejected call, later cry unanswered	Wisdom's hearers refuse her call and later call out without answer; it gives a specific biblical form to the commentary's warning that remembrance and a request for release come too late.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Prov.4.13	instruction is your life	Proverbs calls disciplined instruction life itself; this makes a precise Jewish counterpart to the commentary's claim that accepting the admonition is a response to what gives life.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.5.24	hearing the word, passing from death to life	The one who hears and believes Jesus' word has eternal life and has passed from death to life; it directly parallels the commentary's spiritual use of life for a person who receives the warning.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Eph.2.5	dead in transgressions, made alive with Christ	Ephesians says those dead through transgressions are made alive with Christ; it offers a concrete Christian use of death and life as present moral-spiritual conditions beneath the commentary's final outcome.
+medium	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:1Tim.5.6	dead while living	The self-indulgent person is said to be dead while living, a Christian moral metaphor that resembles an in-between state; the commentary instead stresses that 87:13 negates both exits without calling its victim merely half-dead.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.16.31	not hearing Moses and prophets	The rich man's requested warning is refused on the ground that those who do not hear Moses and the prophets will not be persuaded even by resurrection; it joins refused warning to an irreversible postmortem setting as the commentary does.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Deut.32.2	teaching as rain and speech as dew on grass	Moses compares teaching to rain and speech to dew upon grass; this directly links the commentary's rain-and-living-pasture imagery with admonition that nourishes rather than the fire that consumes.
+strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.5.24	rejected Torah, stubble consumed by fire	Isaiah joins rejection of YHWH's Torah to roots rotting and stubble consumed by fire; its warning, vegetation, and fire form a particularly close triad beside the commentary's avoidance of reminder and grass-to-fire imagery.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.37.14	Spirit placed in the dead so they live	God promises to put his spirit in Israel's dry bones so that they live; it is the positive prophetic counterpart to the commentary's layered account of life as more than continued sensation.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ps.1.3	Torah-hearer as a watered fruitful tree	The person who meditates on Torah is like a tree by streams that bears fruit; this gives the commentary's admonition, flourishing vegetation, and living-versus-barren moral contrast a biblical form.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.40.8	grass withers but God's word stands forever	Isaiah contrasts withering grass with the enduring divine word; it clarifies the commentary's movement from short worldly life and fading pasture toward what is lasting.
+strong	tevrat	motif	Mishnah Avot 4:17	life of this world and bliss of the world to come	Rabbi Jacob compares the whole life of this world with the superior bliss of the world to come; this is a close rabbinic counterpart to the commentary's contrast between preferred near life and the more abiding life.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Mark.8.36	gaining the world and forfeiting one's life	Jesus asks what profit comes from gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life; it gives a sharp Gospel analogue to the commentary's claim that preferring the near life forfeits the true one.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1Tim.6.19	the life that is truly life	Paul urges storing treasure for the future in order to seize the life that is truly life; its explicit distinction between apparent present possession and real life closely matches the commentary's account of the enduring afterlife.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Gen.3.19	earth, dust, and return to dust	Adam is told that he came from dust and will return to it; this grounds the commentary's contrast between earth as the place of ordinary life and death and fire as the place where neither transition occurs.

strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Luke.16.24	conscious anguish in flame	The rich man remains conscious and cries out that he is in anguish in flame; this supplies a narrated Christian analogue for the commentary's insistence that fire's occupant is not extinguished by suffering.

strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Matt.25.46	eternal punishment and eternal life	Matthew's final judgment places eternal punishment and eternal life in one antithetical sentence, a close frame for the commentary's contrast between enduring torment and the real, lasting life denied to it.

strong	tevrat	motif	WLC:Dan.12.2	awakening to everlasting life or contempt	Daniel's sleepers awake either to everlasting life or everlasting contempt; this gives a biblical two-outcome resurrection frame for the commentary's opposition between full afterlife and enduring punitive condition.

strong	incil	paralel	SBLGNT:Rev.1.18	the living one became dead and lives forever	The risen Jesus names himself the living one who became dead and is alive forever; this compact death-life-resurrection sequence is the positive inverse of 87:13's suspended condition.
strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Rom.6.9	raised Christ dies no more	Paul says that the risen Christ dies no more and death no longer rules him; it provides a Christian account of deathlessness joined to actual life, precisely the conjunction the commentary says hell lacks.

medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Ezek.37.14	Spirit placed in the dead so they live	God promises to put his spirit in Israel's dry bones so that they live; it is the positive prophetic counterpart to the commentary's layered account of life as more than continued sensation.

+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.12.25	loving present life loses it, preserving life eternal	Jesus says that clinging to one's life in this world loses it, while relinquishing it preserves it for eternal life; this is a sharp Gospel analogue to the commentary's preferred near life versus the lasting life.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:John.6.27	perishing food and food abiding to eternal life	Jesus contrasts food that perishes with food that remains for eternal life; it specifically supports the commentary's contrast of a short chosen worldly provision with a durable, real life.
+strong	incil	motif	SBLGNT:1John.3.14	passing from death to life, remaining in death	Love is said to mark passage from death to life, while lack of love leaves one in death; this offers another concrete Christian use of life and death as moral-spiritual states before final judgment.

+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.57.2	righteous dead enter peace and rest	The upright person who dies enters peace and rests; this offers a prophetic positive counterpart to the commentary's secondary reading of death as stillness and rest, both withheld from the fire's inhabitant.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Amos.8.12	seeking YHWH's word but not finding it	Amos foresees people wandering in search of YHWH's word and not finding it; it gives a concrete prophetic form to the commentary's too-late remembrance after the time for hearing has passed.
+medium	tevrat	motif	WLC:Isa.38.19	the living give thanks, unlike the dead	Hezekiah says that the living, not the dead, give thanks to God; it clarifies the commentary's association of life with responsive remembrance and worship rather than bare continued sensation.
+medium	tevrat	motif	Wisdom of Solomon 3:3	the righteous dead are in peace	Wisdom says that those who seemed to die are in peace; this Jewish reflection makes death a secure state for the righteous, a deliberate opposite to the fire where the sufferer receives neither death nor peace.
+medium	tevrat	yorum_gelenegi	Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1	no share in the world to come for denial of resurrection	The Mishnah excludes from the world to come those who deny resurrection from the Torah and related fundamentals; this rabbinic rule concretely links rejection of revealed truth with loss of future life, as the commentary's warning logic does.
+medium	tevrat	paralel	Josephus, Antiquities 18.116-119	John's moral exhortation and execution by Herod	Josephus portrays John as exhorting justice and piety before Herod has him killed; this Jewish witness supplies historical narrative context for the commentary's righteous Yahya and distinguishes ordinary mortal death from the fire's deathless condition.
+medium	incil	paralel	Arabic Infancy Gospel, opening cradle-speech (chapter numbering varies)	newborn Jesus speaks from the cradle	The opening scene of the Arabic Infancy Gospel has the newborn Jesus speak from the cradle; its setting differs from the Qur'anic defense of Mary, but it is a specific Christian infancy parallel to the extraordinary cradle-speech invoked in the commentary.
+medium	incil	karsi_anlati	SBLGNT:Acts.3.23	refusal to hear the prophet brings destruction	Acts says that every person refusing to hear the promised prophet will be destroyed from the people; it shares the commentary's warning-and-refusal logic but uses destruction where 87:13 depicts an unended condition without death.
+medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Heb.2.3	no escape after neglecting salvation	Hebrews asks how people can escape after neglecting such a great salvation; this concise warning formula parallels the commentary's closed possibility of escape after the reminder has been evaded.
+medium	incil	motif	SBLGNT:Luke.15.24	dead and alive again, lost and found	The returning son is declared dead and alive again, lost and found; this recovery scene is a narrative positive counterpart to the commentary's moral death-life language and its final absence of a way back.
*** End Patch";

text(typeof r === "string" ? r : JSON.stringify(r));
